title: Part 2, Chapter 1
paragraphs: He lay there for a very long time. Now and then he seemed to wake, and at those moments noticed that it was deep into the night, but it didn't occur to him to get up. Finally he noticed it was starting to get light. He was lying on his back, still dazed from his stupor. Fearful, desperate shrieks rose from the street -- sounds he heard every night under his window after two o'clock. They woke him now.
"Ah, the drunks are pouring out of the taverns," he thought. "It's past two." And he immediately leapt up, as though someone had yanked him off the sofa.
"What! Past two o'clock!"
He sat down on the sofa -- and instantly remembered everything. All at once, in a single flash, he remembered everything.

For the first moment he thought he was going mad. A terrible chill seized him -- but it was the fever that had started long before, while he slept. Now violent shivering gripped him so hard that his teeth chattered and his whole body shook. He opened the door and listened. The entire building was asleep. He stared in amazement at himself and at everything around the room, wondering how he could have come home the night before without locking the door, thrown himself on the sofa without undressing, without even taking off his hat. It had fallen off and lay on the floor near his pillow.
"If anyone had come in, what would they have thought? That I was drunk, but..."

He rushed to the window. There was enough light, and he frantically began examining himself from head to foot -- all his clothes. Were there traces? But he couldn't do it that way. Shaking with cold, he started stripping off everything and examining each piece again. He went through every thread and scrap, and, not trusting himself, repeated the search three times.

There seemed to be nothing -- no trace -- except in one spot, where thick drops of dried blood clung to the frayed edge of his trousers. He grabbed a large clasp knife and cut off the frayed threads. There seemed to be nothing else.

Suddenly he remembered that the purse and the things he'd taken from the old woman's strongbox were still in his pockets! He hadn't thought until now of taking them out and hiding them! He hadn't even thought about them while checking his clothes! He rushed to pull everything out and throw it on the table. When he'd emptied his pockets and turned them inside out to make sure nothing remained, he carried the whole pile to the corner. The wallpaper had peeled away from the bottom of the wall and hung in tatters. He began stuffing everything into the hole behind the paper. "They're in! Out of sight, purse and all!" he thought with glee, standing up and staring blankly at the hole, which now bulged out more than ever. Suddenly he shuddered with horror. "My God!" he whispered in despair. "What's wrong with me? Is that hidden? Is that any way to hide things?"
He hadn't counted on having trinkets to conceal. He'd only thought about money and hadn't prepared a hiding place.
"What am I even glad about?" he thought. "Is that hiding things? I'm losing my mind -- plain and simple!"

He collapsed onto the sofa in exhaustion, immediately shaken by another unbearable fit of shivering. Mechanically he pulled his old student's winter coat from the chair beside him -- still warm despite being practically in rags -- covered himself with it, and sank again into drowsiness and delirium. He lost consciousness.
No more than five minutes passed before he leapt up again, and in a frenzy pounced on his clothes once more.
"How could I have fallen asleep again with nothing taken care of? Yes, yes -- I didn't remove the loop from the armhole! I forgot -- forgot something like that! A piece of evidence like that!"
He ripped out the loop, hurriedly cut it to pieces, and stuffed the bits among his linen under the pillow.

"Pieces of torn linen can't arouse suspicion, whatever happens. I don't think so, I don't think so, anyway!" he repeated, standing in the middle of the room. With agonizing concentration he began scanning everything around him again -- the floor, every surface -- trying to make sure he'd missed nothing. The growing conviction that all his faculties, even his memory, even the simplest capacity for thought, were failing him, had become an unbearable torment.
"Is it starting already? Is this my punishment? It is!"
The frayed scraps he'd cut from his trousers were lying on the floor in the middle of the room, where anyone walking in would see them!
"What is wrong with me!" he cried again, like a man losing his mind.

Then a strange thought entered his head: perhaps his clothes were covered in blood, perhaps there were stains everywhere, but he couldn't see them, couldn't notice them because his perception was failing, disintegrating... his reason was clouding over.... He suddenly remembered that the purse had blood on it too. "Ah! Then there must be blood on the pocket lining, since I shoved the wet purse in my pocket!"
In a flash he turned the pocket inside out, and -- yes! -- there were traces, stains on the pocket lining!

"So my mind hasn't completely deserted me -- I still have some sense and memory, since I figured this out myself," he thought triumphantly, breathing a deep sigh of relief. "It's just the weakness of fever, a moment's delirium." He ripped the entire lining out of his left trouser pocket. At that instant, sunlight fell on his left boot. On the sock poking out from it, he thought he saw traces! He flung off the boots. "Traces! The tip of the sock was soaked with blood." He must have accidentally stepped in that pool.... "But what do I do with this now? Where do I put the sock, the scraps, the pocket lining?"
He gathered it all in his hands and stood in the middle of the room.

"In the stove? But they'd search the stove first. Burn them? But with what? I don't even have matches. No, better to go out and throw it all away somewhere. Yes, throw it away," he repeated, sinking onto the sofa. "Right now, this instant, without delay..."
But his head dropped onto the pillow instead. The unbearable icy shivering overtook him again. He pulled his coat over himself.

For a long time, for hours, he was tormented by the urge to "go somewhere right now, this second, and get rid of it all, get it out of sight and done with -- right now, right now!" Several times he tried to get up from the sofa but couldn't.
He was finally jolted awake by violent pounding on his door.
"Open up! Are you dead or alive in there? All he does is sleep!" Nastasya shouted, banging with her fist. "Days on end, snoring away like a dog! A dog is what he is! Open up, I said! It's past ten."
"Maybe he's not home," said a man's voice.
"That's the porter's voice.... What does he want?"
He shot upright on the sofa. His heart was hammering painfully.
"Then who latched the door?" Nastasya retorted. "Now he's started bolting himself in! As if anyone would want to steal from him! Open up, you idiot -- wake up!"
"What do they want? Why the porter? It's all been discovered. Resist or open? Whatever happens!..."
He half rose, leaned forward, and unlatched the door.
His room was so small he could reach the latch without getting out of bed. Sure enough -- the porter and Nastasya were standing there.
Nastasya stared at him strangely. He met the porter's gaze with a look that was both defiant and desperate. The porter silently held out a gray folded paper sealed with wax.
"A notice from the office," he announced, handing him the paper.
"What office?"
"A summons to the police station, obviously. You know which office."
"The police?... What for?..."
"How should I know? You're summoned, so go."
The man studied him carefully, glanced around the room, and turned to leave.
"He's seriously ill!" Nastasya observed, not taking her eyes off him. The porter looked back for a moment. "He's had a fever since yesterday," she added.

Raskolnikov said nothing, holding the paper without opening it. "You shouldn't get up, then," Nastasya went on sympathetically, seeing him lower his feet from the sofa. "You're sick, so don't go. There's no rush. What's that you're holding?"

He looked down. In his right hand he was clutching the scraps he'd cut from his trousers, the sock, and the rags of the pocket lining. He had fallen asleep holding them. Thinking about it later, he remembered that half-waking in his fever, he had grabbed all of it tightly and fallen asleep again.
"Look at the rags he's been collecting -- sleeps with them like they're treasure...."
Nastasya dissolved into her hysterical giggling.

He instantly shoved everything under his coat and fixed his eyes intently on her. Incapable as he was of rational thought at that moment, he sensed that nobody would behave this way with a person about to be arrested. "But... the police?"
"You should have some tea! Want some? I'll bring it -- there's some left."
"No... I'm going. I'll go right now," he muttered, getting to his feet.
"You'll never make it downstairs!"
"Yes, I'll go."
"Suit yourself."
She followed the porter out.
He immediately rushed to the light to examine the sock and the scraps.

"There are stains, but barely noticeable -- covered in grime, rubbed, already discolored. Nobody without prior suspicion could make anything of them. Nastasya couldn't have noticed from that distance, thank God!" Then, trembling, he broke the seal on the notice and began reading. It took him a long time to understand. It was an ordinary summons from the district police station, requiring him to appear that day at half past nine at the office of the district superintendent.
"But when has this ever happened? I've never had anything to do with the police! And why today?" he thought in agonized bewilderment. "God, just let it be over quickly!"
He was about to drop to his knees and pray, but burst out laughing instead -- not at the idea of prayer, but at himself.
He began dressing in a hurry. "If I'm done for, I'm done for -- I don't care! Should I put the sock on?" he suddenly wondered. "It'll just get more dirt on it and the traces will disappear."

But the moment he pulled the sock on, he ripped it off again in loathing and horror. He pulled it off, but then, reflecting that he had no other socks, he picked it up and put it back on -- and laughed again.

"It's all just convention, all relative, just a way of looking at things," he thought in a flash, but only on the surface of his mind, while his whole body shuddered. "There -- I got it on! I ended up putting it on after all!"
But the laughter was quickly followed by despair.

"No, this is too much for me..." he thought. His legs were shaking. "From fear," he muttered. His head was spinning and throbbing with fever. "It's a trap! They want to lure me there and trip me up on everything," he thought as he went down the stairs. "The worst part is I'm practically delirious... I might blurt out something stupid..."

On the stairs he remembered that he was leaving everything exactly where it was, in the hole in the wall. "They're probably doing this on purpose -- to search the place while I'm gone," he thought, and stopped short. But such despair possessed him, such a cynicism of misery, that he waved his hand and kept going. "Just get it over with!"

In the street the heat was unbearable again. Not a drop of rain had fallen in all these days. Again dust, bricks, plaster. Again the stench from the shops and taverns, the drunks, the Finnish peddlers, the decrepit cabs. The sun blazed directly in his eyes, making them ache, and his head started spinning -- the way it does for a feverish man stepping into bright sunlight.
When he reached the turning into _that_ street, he looked down it in an agony of dread... at _that_ building... and immediately averted his eyes.
"If they question me, maybe I'll just tell them everything," he thought as he neared the police station.

The station was about a quarter mile away. It had recently moved to new rooms on the fourth floor of a new building. He'd been briefly to the old office once, long ago. Turning through the gateway, he saw a flight of stairs on the right, which a peasant was climbing with a ledger in his hand. "A building porter, most likely -- so the office is up there." He began climbing the stairs, not wanting to ask anyone for directions.
"I'll go in, fall on my knees, and confess everything..." he thought as he reached the fourth floor.

The staircase was steep, narrow, and slippery with dirty water. The apartment kitchens opened onto the stairs and stood open nearly all day, producing a terrible smell and heat. The staircase was crowded with porters going up and down with their ledgers, policemen, and people of every sort and both genders. The office door also stood wide open. Peasants waited inside. The heat in there was stifling too, with a nauseating smell of fresh paint and stale oil from the newly renovated rooms.

After waiting briefly, he decided to move forward into the next room. All the rooms were small with low ceilings. A terrible impatience drove him on. No one paid any attention to him. In the second room, some clerks sat writing, dressed hardly better than he was -- a rather odd-looking bunch. He approached one of them.
"What do you want?"
He held out the notice.
"You're a student?" the man asked, glancing at the paper.
"Yes, a former student."
The clerk looked at him with zero interest. He was a particularly unkempt individual with the glazed look of a man consumed by a single fixed idea.
"I won't get anything out of this one -- he has no interest in anything," Raskolnikov thought.
"Go in there, to the head clerk," the man said, pointing toward the farthest room.

He went into that room -- the fourth in a row -- a small room packed with people who were somewhat better dressed than those in the outer rooms. Among them were two women. One, poorly dressed in mourning, sat at the table across from the head clerk, writing something at his dictation. The other was a very stout, florid woman with a purplish-red, blotchy face, extravagantly overdressed, wearing a brooch on her bosom the size of a saucer. She was standing to one side, apparently waiting. Raskolnikov thrust his notice at the head clerk. The clerk glanced at it, said "One moment," and went back to attending to the woman in mourning.
He breathed more easily. "It can't be about _that_."
Gradually he began to regain his composure, urging himself to stay calm and courageous.

"Some stupid slip, some trivial carelessness, and I could give myself away! Hmm... it's a shame there's no air in here," he added. "So stuffy.... Making my head spin even worse... and my thoughts too..."

He was aware of terrible inner turmoil. He was afraid of losing self-control. He tried to grab onto something, fix his mind on something completely unrelated, but couldn't manage it at all. Yet the head clerk fascinated him -- he kept hoping to read him, to guess something from his face.

He was a very young man, about twenty-two, with a dark, animated face that looked older than his years. He was fashionably and foppishly dressed, with his hair parted in the middle, carefully combed and pomaded. He wore several rings on his well-groomed fingers and a gold chain across his waistcoat. He had even exchanged a couple of words in French with a foreigner in the room, and said them fairly correctly.

"Luise Ivanovna, please sit down," he said casually to the brightly dressed, purple-faced lady, who was still standing as though she didn't dare take a seat, though there was a chair right beside her.

"Ich danke," she replied, and softly, with a rustle of silk, sank into the chair. Her light blue dress trimmed with white lace billowed around the table like a hot-air balloon, filling nearly half the room. She reeked of perfume. But she was clearly embarrassed about taking up so much space and smelling so strongly, and though her smile was simultaneously insolent and servile, it betrayed obvious unease.

The woman in mourning finished up and stood. Suddenly an officer strode in with a jaunty, self-important swagger of his shoulders at each step. He tossed his cockaded cap on the table and dropped into an armchair. The stout little lady practically jumped out of her seat, bobbing in a frenzy of curtsies, but the officer took absolutely no notice of her, and she didn't dare sit down again in his presence. He was the assistant superintendent. He had a reddish mustache sticking out horizontally on each side of his face, and extremely small features that expressed nothing much except a certain arrogance. He shot an irritated sideways glance at Raskolnikov -- who was so badly dressed, and whose bearing, despite his humiliating position, did not match his clothes at all. Raskolnikov had carelessly fixed a long, direct stare on him, and the officer clearly took offense.
"What do you want?" he barked, apparently astounded that such a ragged creature wasn't annihilated by the majesty of his gaze.
"I was summoned... by a notice..." Raskolnikov faltered.

"It's about the recovery of a debt -- from _the student_," the head clerk cut in hurriedly, tearing himself from his papers. "Here!" He flung a document at Raskolnikov and pointed to the relevant section. "Read this!"
"Money? What money?" Raskolnikov thought. "But... then... it's definitely not _that_."
He trembled with joy. A sudden, intense, indescribable relief flooded through him. A weight had been lifted from his shoulders.

"And what time were you instructed to appear, sir?" the assistant superintendent shouted, sounding for some unknown reason more and more aggrieved. "It says nine o'clock, and it's already past twelve!"

"The notice was delivered to me just fifteen minutes ago," Raskolnikov answered loudly over his shoulder. To his own surprise, he suddenly felt angry too, and found a certain pleasure in it. "And it's enough that I came here at all, sick with fever."
"Kindly stop shouting!"
"I'm not shouting -- I'm speaking quite calmly. It's you who's shouting at me. I'm a student, and I don't allow anyone to shout at me."
The assistant superintendent was so furious that for a moment he could only sputter. He leapt from his chair.
"Be silent! You are in a government office! Don't be insolent, sir!"
"You're in a government office too," Raskolnikov fired back, "and you're smoking a cigarette while shouting, so you're the one showing disrespect to everyone here."
He felt an indescribable satisfaction at having said this.
The head clerk looked at him with a smile. The furious assistant superintendent was visibly thrown.

"That's none of your business!" he finally shouted with forced volume. "Just sign the declaration as required. Show him, Alexander Grigorievich. A complaint has been filed against you! You don't pay your debts! A fine specimen you are!"
But Raskolnikov had stopped listening. He had seized the document eagerly, desperate for an explanation. He read it once, twice, and still didn't understand.
"What is this?" he asked the head clerk.

"It's a writ for the recovery of money owed on an IOU. You must either pay the full amount including costs and expenses, or submit a written declaration of when you can pay, along with an undertaking not to leave the city without paying and not to sell or conceal your property. The creditor has the right to sell your property and proceed against you according to the law."
"But I... don't owe anyone anything!"

"That's not our concern. An IOU for one hundred and fifteen rubles, legally attested and overdue, given by you to the widow of Assessor Zarnitsyn nine months ago, and subsequently transferred by the widow to a Mr. Chebarov, has been filed with us for recovery. Hence the summons."
"But she's my landlady!"
"And what of it?"

The head clerk regarded him with a condescending smile of pity, tinged with triumph, like someone watching a novice under fire for the first time -- as if to say, "Well, how do you feel now?" But what did any of this matter now -- an IOU, a debt collection? Was it worth worrying about, worth even a moment's attention? He stood there, reading, listening, answering, even asking questions -- all mechanically. The triumphant feeling of safety, of deliverance from overwhelming danger, filled his entire soul at that moment -- without thought for the future, without analysis, without speculation or doubt. It was an instant of total, direct, purely instinctive joy. But right then, something like a thunderstorm erupted in the office. The assistant superintendent, still shaken by Raskolnikov's disrespect, still fuming and obviously intent on salvaging his wounded dignity, pounced on the unfortunate well-dressed lady, who had been gazing at him since he walked in with an extraordinarily silly smile.

"You shameless creature!" he suddenly roared at the top of his voice. (The woman in mourning had already left.) "What was going on in your house last night? Another disgrace! You're a scandal to the whole street! Fighting and drinking again! Do you want the workhouse? I've warned you ten times that I wouldn't let you off an eleventh. And here you are again!"

The paper fell from Raskolnikov's hands. He stared at the smartly dressed lady being berated so roughly. But he quickly understood what was happening and immediately began to find the scene genuinely entertaining. He listened with pleasure -- he wanted to laugh and laugh.... Every nerve was on edge.
"Ilya Petrovich!" the head clerk began anxiously, but stopped, knowing from experience that the enraged assistant could not be stopped except by force.

As for the well-dressed lady, at first she positively trembled before the onslaught. But strangely, the more numerous and violent the insults became, the more amiable her expression grew, and the more seductive the smiles she directed at the terrible assistant. She shifted uncomfortably and curtsied constantly, waiting impatiently for a chance to get a word in. At last she found it.

"There was no noise and no fighting in my house whatsoever, Mr. Captain," she began, like peas rattling from a pan, speaking Russian confidently but with a strong German accent. "And no scandal whatsoever, and his honor arrived drunk -- this is the whole truth, Mr. Captain -- and I am not to blame.... Mine is an honorable house, Mr. Captain, and honorable behavior, Mr. Captain, and I never, never want any scandal. But he came completely drunk and then ordered three more bottles, and then he lifted one leg and began playing the piano with his foot, and that is not at all proper in an honorable house, and he _ganz_ broke the piano, and that is very bad manners, and I told him so. And he picked up a bottle and began hitting everyone with it. And then I called the porter, and Karl came, and he punched Karl in the eye, and he punched Henriette in the eye too, and slapped me five times across the face. And it was so ungentlemanly in an honorable house, Mr. Captain, and I screamed. And he opened the window onto the canal and stood in the window squealing like a little pig. A disgrace! The idea of squealing like a pig out the window into the street! Shame on him! And Karl dragged him away from the window by his coat, and it's true, Mr. Captain, he tore _sein Rock_. And then he screamed that _man muss_ pay him fifteen rubles in damages. And I paid him, Mr. Captain, five rubles for _sein Rock_. And he is a most ungentlemanly visitor and caused the whole scandal. 'I'll write about you,' he said, 'I can write about you in all the newspapers.'"
"So he was a writer?"
"Yes, Mr. Captain, and such an ungentlemanly visitor in an honorable house...."
"Now then! Enough! I've already told you..."
"Ilya Petrovich!" the head clerk said again, pointedly.
The assistant glanced at him quickly. The head clerk gave a slight shake of his head.

"...So I'm telling you this, most respectable Luise Ivanovna, and I'm telling you for the last time," the assistant went on. "If there is one more scandal in your honorable house, I will have you locked up personally -- as they say in polite society. You hear me? So a literary man, a writer, took five rubles for his coat-tail in an 'honorable house'? A fine lot, these writers!" He shot a contemptuous glance at Raskolnikov. "There was a scene in a restaurant the other day too -- a writer ate dinner and refused to pay. 'I'll write a satire about you,' he says. And there was another one on a steamship last week who used the foulest language in front of a civil counselor's wife and daughter, a respectable family. And another got thrown out of a confectioner's just the other day. That's what they're like -- writers, literary types, students, soapbox orators.... Pfah! Get out! I'll come check on you personally. And you'd better watch yourself! You hear?"

And he cast a contemptuous glance at Raskolnikov. "There was a scandal in a restaurant the other day, too. Some writer had eaten his dinner and refused to pay. 'I'll write a satire about you,' he says. And just last week, another one on a steamer used the most disgraceful language toward a respectable civil councillor's family — his wife and daughter. And the other day one of them was thrown out of a confectioner's shop. That's what they're like, these writers, literary types, students, loudmouths... Pfoo! Now get along! I'll come check on you myself one day. Then you'd better watch out! Do you hear?"

With hurried deference, Luise Ivanovna began curtsying in every direction, and curtsied her way right to the door. But at the door she stumbled backwards into a handsome officer with a fresh, open face and magnificent thick fair whiskers. This was the district superintendent himself, Nikodim Fomitch. Luise Ivanovna hastily curtsied almost to the ground and fluttered out of the office with quick, mincing steps.

"Thunder and lightning again — a hurricane!" said Nikodim Fomitch to Ilya Petrovitch in a friendly, civil tone. "You've got yourself all worked up again, fuming away! I could hear it from the stairs!"

"Well, so what!" Ilya Petrovitch drawled with gentlemanly nonchalance, swaggering over to another table with some papers, his shoulders swinging jauntily at each step. "Here, take a look if you will: this writer, or student — he was one at some point, at least — doesn't pay his debts, has given a promissory note, won't vacate his room, constant complaints are lodged against him, and then he has the nerve to protest about my smoking in his presence! He behaves like a cad himself — and just look at him, please. There's the gentleman, and what a fine sight he is!"

"Poverty is no crime, my friend, but we all know you go off like gunpowder — you can't take even the slightest criticism," continued Nikodim Fomitch, turning warmly to Raskolnikov. "I expect you took offence at something and went too far yourself. But you'd be wrong about him; he's a fine fellow, I assure you, just explosive! Gets heated, flares up, boils over, and there's no stopping him! And then it's all over! And underneath it all, a heart of gold! His nickname in the regiment was the Explosive Lieutenant..."
"And what a regiment it was, too," cried Ilya Petrovitch, quite pleased by this friendly banter, though still somewhat sulky.

Raskolnikov suddenly felt an urge to say something exceptionally pleasant to all of them. "Excuse me, Captain," he began casually, turning to Nikodim Fomitch, "please try to understand my situation... I'm ready to apologize if I've been rude. I'm a poor student, sick and worn down by poverty. I've had to stop studying because I can't support myself right now, but I'll be getting money soon. I have a mother and sister in the province of X. They'll send it, and I'll pay what I owe. My landlady is a kind-hearted woman, but she's so frustrated that I've lost my tutoring work and haven't paid her for the last four months that she won't even send up my dinner anymore. And I don't understand this promissory note at all. She's demanding I pay on this note. But how can I pay? You be the judge!"
"But that's not our concern, you know," the head clerk observed.

"Yes, yes, I completely agree. But let me explain..." Raskolnikov went on, still addressing Nikodim Fomich but doing his best to include Ilya Petrovich as well, though the latter persistently pretended to be rummaging through papers, contemptuously ignoring him. "Let me explain that I've been living there for nearly three years, and at first... at first... why should I hide it? -- at the very beginning I promised to marry her daughter. It was a verbal promise, freely given... she was a girl... I actually liked her, though I wasn't in love with her... a youthful thing, in short... What I mean is, my landlady extended me generous credit in those days, and I led a rather... careless life..."

"Nobody's asking for your personal details, sir. We don't have time for this," Ilya Petrovich cut in roughly, with a note of triumph. But Raskolnikov stopped him with sudden heat, though he found it extremely hard to speak.

"Excuse me, excuse me -- let me explain... how things happened... I agree, it's not strictly necessary, but... A year ago, the girl died of typhus. I stayed on as a lodger. When my landlady moved to her current apartment, she told me -- in a friendly way -- that she had complete trust in me, but would I mind giving her an IOU for one hundred and fifteen rubles, the total I owed her? She said that as long as I gave her this paper, she would extend me credit again, as much as I needed, and would never -- those were her exact words -- never make use of the IOU until I could pay on my own... And now, when I've lost my lessons and have nothing to eat, she goes ahead with legal proceedings. What am I supposed to say to that?"

"All these touching details are no business of ours," Ilya Petrovich interrupted rudely. "You need to submit a written declaration, but as for your love affairs and all these tragic episodes, we have nothing to do with that."
"Now, come... you're being harsh," Nikodim Fomich murmured, sitting down at the table and starting to write. He looked a little embarrassed.
"Write!" the head clerk said to Raskolnikov.
"Write what?" he answered gruffly.
"I'll dictate it to you."

Raskolnikov had the impression the head clerk treated him more casually and dismissively after his little speech. But strangely, he suddenly felt completely indifferent to what anyone thought of him, and this change happened in a flash, in a single instant. If he had cared to reflect, he would have been astonished that he could have spoken to them the way he just had a minute ago, pressing his feelings on them. And where had those feelings come from? Now, even if the room had been filled not with police officials but with his closest, dearest friends, he would not have found a single human word for them -- so empty was his heart. A bleak sensation of agonizing, eternal solitude and disconnection crystallized in his soul. It wasn't the pettiness of his sentimental outburst to Ilya Petrovich, or the pettiness of the latter's triumph over him, that caused this sudden reversal. Oh, what did his own humiliation matter now, or all these petty vanities -- the officers, the German women, the debts, the police station? If he had been sentenced to burn at the stake at that moment, he wouldn't have stirred, would barely have heard the sentence through. Something entirely new, sudden, and unprecedented was happening inside him. It wasn't that he understood it, but he felt with all the force of direct sensation that he could never again appeal to these people at the police station with sentimental outpourings like his recent one, or with anything else at all. And even if they had been his own brothers and sisters instead of police officers, there would have been absolutely no point in appealing to them, under any circumstance. He had never experienced such a strange, terrible sensation. And the most agonizing part was this: it was more a feeling than a thought or idea -- a direct sensation, the most agonizing of any he had known in his entire life.

The head clerk began dictating the standard form of declaration -- that he could not pay, that he undertook to do so at a future date, that he would not leave the city, that he would not sell or conceal his property, and so forth.
"But you can barely write -- you can hardly hold the pen," the head clerk observed, looking at Raskolnikov with curiosity. "Are you ill?"
"Yes. Dizzy. Go on!"
"That's all. Sign it."
The head clerk took the paper and turned to other business.

Raskolnikov returned the pen but instead of standing up and leaving, he put his elbows on the table and pressed his head in his hands. It felt like a nail was being driven into his skull. A strange idea suddenly seized him: to stand up right now, walk over to Nikodim Fomich, and tell him everything that happened yesterday -- then go home with him and show him the things in the hole in the corner. The impulse was so strong he actually rose from his seat to act on it. "Shouldn't I think about this for a moment?" flashed through his mind. "No, better to throw off the burden without thinking." But suddenly he stopped, rooted to the spot. Nikodim Fomich was talking animatedly with Ilya Petrovich, and the words reached him:

"Impossible. They'll both be released. To start with, the whole story contradicts itself. Why would they have called the porter if they'd done it? To inform on themselves? As a ruse? No, that would be too clever! Besides, the student Pestryakov was seen at the gate by both porters and a woman as he went in. He was walking with three friends who left him only at the gate, and he asked the porters for directions in their presence. Now, would he have asked for directions if he'd been going there with that kind of intent? As for Koch, he spent half an hour at the silversmith's downstairs before going up to the old woman, and he left the silversmith's at exactly a quarter to eight. Now just consider..."

"But wait -- how do you explain this contradiction? They themselves state that they knocked and the door was locked, but three minutes later, when they went up with the porter, the door turned out to be unlatched."

"That's exactly the point. The murderer must have been inside, bolted in. And they would have caught him for certain if Koch hadn't been a fool and gone down to look for the porter too. The murderer must have used that interval to get downstairs and slip past them somehow. Koch keeps crossing himself, saying: 'If I'd stayed, he would have jumped out and killed me with the axe.' He's going to have a thanksgiving service -- ha ha!"
"And nobody saw the murderer?"
"How could they? The building is a regular Noah's Ark," the head clerk put in.
"It's clear, perfectly clear," Nikodim Fomich said warmly.
"No, it's anything but clear," Ilya Petrovich maintained.
Raskolnikov picked up his hat and walked toward the door, but he didn't make it....

When he regained consciousness, he found himself sitting in a chair, someone supporting him on the right, someone else standing on the left holding a yellowish glass of yellow water, and Nikodim Fomich standing before him, staring at him. He stood up from the chair.
"What's this? Are you ill?" Nikodim Fomich asked rather sharply.
"He could barely hold the pen while signing," the head clerk said, settling back at his desk and returning to his work.

"Have you been sick long?" cried Ilya Petrovich from his desk, where he too had been examining papers. He had naturally come over to look when the sick man fainted, but withdrew the moment he came to.
"Since yesterday," Raskolnikov muttered.
"Did you go out yesterday?"
"Yes."
"Even though you were ill?"
"Yes."
"At what time?"
"Around seven in the evening."
"And where did you go, if I may ask?"
"Down the street."
"Short and sweet."
Raskolnikov, white as a sheet, had answered sharply and curtly, without dropping his dark, feverish eyes from Ilya Petrovich's stare.
"He can barely stand on his feet. And you..." Nikodim Fomich began.
"No matter," Ilya Petrovich said in a peculiar tone.
Nikodim Fomich was about to say something more, but glancing at the head clerk, who was watching him very intently, he fell silent. There was a sudden, strange pause.
"Very well, then," Ilya Petrovich concluded. "We won't detain you."
Raskolnikov walked out. He caught the sound of animated conversation behind him, and above it rose the questioning voice of Nikodim Fomich. Out in the street, his faintness passed completely.
"A search -- they'll search my place right away," he repeated to himself, hurrying home. "The bastards! They suspect me."
His old terror seized him completely once again.
